content: Imagine you have a beautiful ice sculpture. You leave it outside on a hot summer day. When you return, the sculpture is gone, and only a puddle of water remains! But what if you put that puddle back in the freezer?
Is the puddle of water made of something completely different from the ice sculpture? If you freeze the water again, do you get ice back? Think about whether the 'stuff' actually changed.

content.title: Melting Ice to Water
content.description: An animation showing solid ice cubes melting into liquid water, and then freezing back into solid ice cubes, demonstrating that the chemical composition (H2O) remains exactly the same.

content: This is a perfect example of a **Physical Change**. A physical change happens when a substance changes its physical properties (like shape, size, color, or state) but no new substance is formed.

question: If you tear a piece of paper into 100 tiny pieces, what kind of change has occurred?
options: A chemical change because it's no longer useful
A physical change because it is still paper
No change because it is still paper
A chemical change because you cannot stick it back easily

content: Remember: Physical changes are often, but not always, reversible. Tearing paper is irreversible, but it's still a physical change because it's still paper!

Look around your room. Can you find something that you can bend, fold, or stretch? If you change its shape, did it become a completely new material? Explain why folding a shirt is just a physical change.

Physical changes are everywhere in our daily life! When you chop vegetables for dinner, when glass shatters, or when wax melts in a candle—these are all physical changes. The material remains exactly the same, it just looks different.
Mini Challenge: Take a piece of clay or dough. Roll it into a ball, then flatten it into a pancake. Did you create a new substance? No! You've just mastered the concept of a physical change!

Have you ever seen an old bicycle left outside in the rain for months? It turns from shiny silver to a crusty, reddish-brown color. The metal seems to have been eaten away. What exactly happened to it?

Can you wipe away the reddish-brown crust to make the metal shiny again like you wipe dust off a table? Or has the metal itself turned into something entirely new? What do you think this reddish-brown stuff is?

content.title: Rusting of Iron
content.description: An animation showing iron atoms reacting with oxygen atoms from the air and water molecules, binding together to form a completely new structure: iron oxide (rust).

content: The reddish-brown stuff is called **Rust**. This is an example of a **Chemical Change**. A chemical change (or chemical reaction) occurs when one or more substances react to form one or more completely new substances.

question: When you bake a cake, the batter turns into a fluffy sponge. Is this a physical or chemical change?
options: Physical change, because it's still food
Chemical change, because new substances are formed by heat
Physical change, because it just changed its shape
Neither, baking is not a change

content: Many students think that boiling water to make steam is a chemical change because a gas is formed. But steam is still water (H2O)! It's a physical change. A chemical change always makes a completely NEW substance.
Think about when a piece of wood burns into ash and smoke. Can you turn the ash back into wood? Chemical changes are usually irreversible. Why do you think it's impossible to 'un-burn' something?

Chemical changes are the reason we have life! Digestion of food in our bodies, ripening of fruits, and even photosynthesis in plants are all chemical changes. The ancient Indian science of Ayurveda heavily relies on understanding how herbs undergo chemical changes to make medicines.

Mini Challenge: The Vinegar and Baking Soda Volcano! If you mix baking soda and vinegar, they bubble up vigorously. This is a chemical change producing a new gas called Carbon Dioxide. Try to find other examples of gas being produced in your kitchen!
Have you ever seen massive, beautiful salt crystals near the ocean, or glittering rock candy? How does a solid, beautiful crystal form out of completely clear, liquid water?

If you dissolve salt in water, the salt disappears. If you boil all the water away, what do you think is left behind in the pot? Is it a new chemical, or is it just the original salt returning to solid form?

content.title: The Process of Crystallisation
content.description: An animation showing water evaporating from a saturated copper sulphate solution, leaving behind copper sulphate molecules that slowly pack together into perfect geometric blue crystals.

content: The process of obtaining large, pure crystals of a substance from its solution is called **Crystallisation**. Even though a crystal looks magical, crystallisation is actually just a **Physical Change**, because no new substance is formed!

question: Which of the following is true about Crystallisation?
options: It is a chemical change because crystals look completely different.
It is a physical change because only the state and shape change, not the substance.
It is a chemical change because heat is used to evaporate water.
It creates a completely new substance called 'crystal'.

content: If you take a blue copper sulphate crystal and crush it into fine powder, it doesn't look like a crystal anymore. But is it still copper sulphate? Explain how the shape of a material doesn't change its true identity.

Crystallisation is used in the real world to purify things. For example, the salt we get from seawater contains many impurities. Through crystallisation, we separate the pure salt from the dirty seawater so we can eat it!

Mini Challenge: Ask an adult to help you dissolve sugar in hot water until no more dissolves. Hang a string in it and wait a few days. You will master crystallisation by growing your own rock candy crystals!
